questions.stem: Why does a hospital need a water management program that includes the building's internal plumbing rather than focusing only on outdoor fountains or cooling towers?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Legionella can grow and spread in complex building water systems, and healthcare facilities often serve people at high risk for Legionnaires' disease.","B":"Legionella is limited to decorative outdoor water features and does not grow in building plumbing.","C":"Municipal treatment guarantees that Legionella cannot multiply after water enters a building.","D":"Water management programs are designed only to manage drinking-water taste and odor."}}
questions.rationale: CDC recommends comprehensive water management programs for healthcare facilities because complex building water systems can support Legionella growth and transmission and healthcare facilities serve vulnerable populations. Water management therefore includes internal plumbing and relevant devices, not only outdoor water features.
questions.source_name: CDC — Water Management in Healthcare Facilities
questions.source_detail: March 15, 2024: healthcare facilities should develop and implement comprehensive water management programs to reduce Legionella growth and transmission; building water systems and vulnerable populations are central risk considerations.

questions.stem: A hospital receives an FDA medical-device recall notice for equipment currently in use. What is the most appropriate initial facility response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Identify affected devices and follow the recall-specific correction or removal instructions and the facility's recall procedure.","B":"Automatically discard every recalled device because every FDA recall requires permanent removal.","C":"Continue using every recalled device until it fails because a recall is only informational.","D":"Ignore the recall unless a patient has already been injured."}}
questions.rationale: FDA defines a medical-device recall as a correction or removal action. A recall does not always require stopping use or returning the device; some recalls require inspection, adjustment, repair, labeling changes, or other correction. The facility should identify affected inventory and follow the specific recall instructions and its internal response process.
questions.source_name: FDA — What Is a Medical Device Recall?
questions.source_detail: Current FDA page: a recall may involve correction or removal; it does not always mean the product must be stopped or returned and can require checking, adjusting, or fixing the device.

questions.stem: Which instruction is part of respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette in a healthcare setting?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, dispose of used tissues, and perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.","B":"Cough openly if symptoms are mild because source control is unnecessary.","C":"Reuse contaminated tissues throughout the visit to reduce waste.","D":"Skip hand hygiene after coughing if a tissue was used."}}
questions.rationale: CDC includes respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette within Standard Precautions. Symptomatic people should contain respiratory secretions by covering the mouth and nose, use and dispose of tissues, and clean their hands after contact with respiratory secretions.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guideline for Isolation Precautions, Respiratory Hygiene/Cough Etiquette
questions.source_detail: Summary Recommendations IV.C.2.a and Appendix A Table 4: cover mouth/nose when coughing or sneezing, use/dispose tissues, and perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.

questions.stem: A hospital is considering reprocessing a device originally labeled for single use. Which statement is accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Some single-use devices can be legally reprocessed, but the reprocessor must meet applicable FDA requirements and demonstrate that the device can be safely and effectively reprocessed.","B":"Every single-use device can be reprocessed without validation or regulatory oversight.","C":"FDA prohibits reprocessing of every device labeled for single use.","D":"Hospitals that reprocess single-use devices are exempt from manufacturer-type FDA requirements."}}
questions.rationale: FDA states that not all single-use devices are suitable for reprocessing, but some can be shown safe and effective through validated reprocessing. Third-party and hospital reprocessors are regulated as manufacturers and must meet applicable premarket, labeling, quality-system, and postmarket requirements.
questions.source_name: FDA — Reprocessing Single-Use Medical Devices: Information for Health Care Facilities
questions.source_detail: Current FDA guidance: not all SUDs are suitable for reprocessing; certain SUDs may be demonstrated safe/effective through validation; healthcare-facility reprocessors are subject to applicable manufacturer requirements.

questions.stem: Why do nurse staffing committees include direct-care nurse representation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"To incorporate frontline knowledge of patient acuity, care needs, and staff skills into unit staffing plans.","B":"To exclude bedside nurses from staffing decisions.","C":"To create one fixed staffing number that ignores patient acuity and unit conditions.","D":"To transfer all staffing authority to personnel with no direct patient-care experience."}}
questions.rationale: ANA describes staffing committees as nurse-led groups that create unit-level staffing plans based on patient acuity and needs matched with staff skills and experience, and supports substantial direct-care nurse representation. Frontline input is therefore an intended safety feature of this model.
questions.source_name: American Nurses Association — Advocating for Safe Staffing in Nursing
questions.source_detail: Staffing committees: nurse-led groups create unit-level staffing plans based on patient population acuity/needs and staff skills/experience; ANA supports direct-care nurse representation.

questions.stem: A fire starts inside a hospital and threatens a patient-care area. Which principle should guide the unit's response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Activate and follow the facility's emergency action and fire-response plan, including its alarm, evacuation or relocation procedures, and assigned staff responsibilities.","B":"Use the same improvised response for every incident because written emergency plans are unnecessary for fires.","C":"Wait for the fire to spread before initiating the facility emergency plan.","D":"Treat the event only as an external mass-casualty influx and ignore internal evacuation procedures."}}
questions.rationale: The prior item relied on a loose 'internal versus external disaster' label. OSHA hospital fire-safety guidance instead supports a concrete emergency-action-plan response: reporting/alarm procedures, evacuation or escape routes, assigned duties, and trained personnel. CMS emergency preparedness likewise uses an all-hazards approach that includes fires and loss of facility operations.
questions.source_name: OSHA — Hospitals: Fire Safety and Emergency Action Plans
questions.source_detail: Hospital fire-safety guidance requires applicable emergency action planning; 29 CFR 1910.38 plan elements include reporting fires, evacuation procedures/escape routes, critical-operation duties, accountability, rescue/medical duties, and responsible contacts.

questions.stem: A client and clinician are choosing among several reasonable treatments. What best describes shared decision making?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The clinician explains evidence, benefits, harms, and options while the client shares values, goals, preferences, and circumstances, and they work together on the decision.","B":"The clinician makes the decision alone and avoids discussing alternatives.","C":"The client receives no clinical guidance and must choose entirely alone.","D":"Shared decision making is appropriate only when there is exactly one possible treatment."}}
questions.rationale: AHRQ defines shared decision making as a collaborative process in which patients and clinicians make decisions informed by evidence, clinician knowledge and experience, and the patient's values, goals, preferences, and circumstances.
questions.source_detail: Current AHRQ definition: collaborative process involving evidence, care-team knowledge/experience, and patient values, goals, preferences and circumstances.

questions.stem: A client with complex chronic illness is assigned a professional case manager. Which activity is most consistent with case management practice?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Coordinate services and resources across the continuum of care to support client goals, continuity, and safe transitions.","B":"Replace every other healthcare professional involved in the client's care.","C":"Make all decisions without client participation.","D":"Provide only bedside procedures and avoid coordination with other services."}}
questions.rationale: CMSA's Standards of Practice frame case management as a professional, client-centered process across the healthcare continuum. Coordination, communication, resource linkage, transitions, and advocacy are core functions rather than replacing other clinicians or excluding the client.
questions.source_name: Case Management Society of America — Standards of Case Management Practice
questions.source_detail: 2022 Standards of Practice with 2024 DEIB/Health Equity addendum; case-management process supports client-centered coordination and continuity across the healthcare continuum.

questions.stem: An adult with decision-making capacity understands the recommended inpatient treatment and its risks but insists on leaving the hospital. What is the best response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Respect the informed refusal, communicate the risks and alternatives, document the discussion and capacity assessment, and provide the safest feasible discharge and follow-up plan.","B":"Physically detain the client solely because the healthcare team believes leaving is unwise.","C":"Assume that choosing to leave automatically proves lack of decision-making capacity.","D":"Require a signed AMA form as the only necessary step and omit the informed-refusal discussion."}}
questions.rationale: A capable adult can refuse recommended treatment even when clinicians consider the choice unsafe. Informed refusal is a process rather than merely a signature: assess capacity, explain risks, benefits and alternatives, document the discussion, and reduce harm through a safe-as-feasible discharge/follow-up plan. Facility policy and applicable law still apply.
questions.source_name: AMA Journal of Ethics — Ethically Informed Discharge Planning and Informed Refusal
questions.source_detail: AMA ethics discussion: adults with decision-making capacity may refuse treatment; holding a capable patient may constitute false imprisonment. Informed refusal requires capacity assessment, information about consequences, and documentation rather than relying only on an AMA form.

questions.stem: A hospital uses a restraint for violent or self-destructive behavior in an adult. Which statement about the order is accurate under the federal hospital Conditions of Participation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The order is time limited; for an adult, each order may be renewed for up to 4 hours, with continued reassessment and all other regulatory requirements still applying.","B":"One restraint order remains valid indefinitely as long as staff document agitation.","C":"A restraint order for violent behavior can routinely be written for 30 days.","D":"Federal requirements permit standing or PRN restraint orders for violent behavior."}}
questions.rationale: 42 CFR 482.13 requires restraint or seclusion for violent or self-destructive behavior to be ordered by an authorized practitioner and limits renewal periods by age. For adults age 18 or older, an order may be renewed up to 4 hours at a time, subject to the regulation's reassessment, monitoring, face-to-face evaluation, discontinuation, and state-law requirements. Standing or PRN restraint orders are not permitted.
questions.source_name: eCFR — 42 CFR §482.13, Condition of Participation: Patient's Rights
questions.source_detail: §482.13(e), restraint/seclusion: no standing or PRN orders; violent/self-destructive behavior renewal limits include 4 hours for adults age 18 or older, with continued monitoring and reassessment requirements.
